summary: Describes a Transport Security Model for SNMP, which lets SNMP take its security identity from a secure underlying transport. It also defines part of the MIB for monitoring and managing that model.

eli5.summary: Instead of SNMP proving who you are on its own, it trusts the locked tunnel it travels through. This explains how it does that.

questions: what is the snmp transport security model
how does tsm differ from usm
subtitle: An SNMP security model that takes the sender's identity and protection level from a secure transport instead of doing its own cryptography.

tldr.problem: SNMP needed a security model that works with secure transports such as SSH, reusing existing security infrastructure, without changing the SNMP architecture or the underlying security protocol.
tldr.mechanism: The Transport Security Model (TSM, security model number 4) reads the authenticated identity and security level from the tmStateReference cache, builds the securityName, checks the level, and defines a small MIB module with a prefix switch and four error counters.
tldr.outcome: SNMPv3 messages can be secured by the transport while SNMP applications still see a normal securityName and securityLevel. The RFC is an Internet Standard and TSM works only with Transport Models that understand tmStateReference.

today: RFC 5591 is an Internet Standard from June 2009 and has not been obsoleted. It builds on the Transport Subsystem of RFC 5590 and names the Secure Shell Transport Model of RFC 5592 as an example of a compatible Transport Model.

sections.title: Introduction and Constraints
sections.content:
RFC 5591 describes a Transport Security Model (TSM) for SNMP, for use with secure Transport Models in the Transport Subsystem defined in RFC 5590. It also defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for monitoring and managing the model. The aim is to use existing, commonly deployed security infrastructures and to minimize implementation and deployment cost.

The design follows five constraints. In times of network stress, the security protocol SHOULD NOT depend solely on services such as NTP or AAA. When the network is not under stress it MAY depend on them. It might not be possible to tell when the network is stressed. A Security Model SHOULD NOT require changes to the SNMP architecture, and SHOULD NOT require changes to the underlying security protocol.
sections.eli5: This is a rulebook for a new kind of name-checker at the SNMP mail room. It has to work with locks that already exist, and keep working when the network is having a bad day.

sections.title: How TSM Fits the Architecture
sections.content:
TSM sits in the Security Subsystem and uses a secure Transport Model. For incoming messages the Transport Model passes a tmStateReference cache. TSM creates the securityName and securityLevel for applications and checks that the tmTransportSecurityLevel reported by the transport is at least as strong as the securityLevel requested by the Message Processing Model. For outgoing messages TSM creates (or reuses) a tmStateReference and passes it to the Transport Model.

TSM provides no authentication or encryption of its own. Which threats are covered depends on the Transport Model, and it trusts that the transport was configured to be at least as strong as it reports. It cannot test those claims. The three levels it deals with are noAuthNoPriv, authNoPriv and authPriv.

On coexistence, SNMPv1 and SNMPv2c message processing always selects the SNMPv1 and SNMPv2c Security Models, so those messages cannot use TSM. For SNMPv3, a msgSecurityModel value of transportSecurityModel(4) directs processing to TSM, and an application sending a message MUST specify that value. TSM keeps its own MIB module, so it can coexist with USM, and it MUST only be used with Transport Models that know how to process a tmStateReference, such as the Secure Shell Transport Model of RFC 5592.
sections.eli5: The name-checker does not make locks. It reads the name tag and lock rating the tunnel reports, and trusts that the tunnel was set up properly.

sections.title: Processing Outgoing Messages
sections.content:
When TSM builds an outgoing message there are two cases. For a Response or Report, a securityStateReference exists, and TSM extracts the cached tmStateReference. It sets tmRequestedSecurityLevel to the cached tmTransportSecurityLevel and sets tmSameSecurity to true, so the response uses the same security as the request.

For a request or notification there is no such reference, so TSM creates a cache with the transport domain, transport address and requested level, and sets tmSameSecurity to false. If snmpTsmConfigurationUsePrefix is false, tmSecurityName is the securityName. If it is true, TSM looks up the prefix for the transport domain. A failed lookup increments snmpTsmUnknownPrefixes. A missing, mismatched or wrong-length prefix (not 1 to 4 characters) increments snmpTsmInvalidPrefixes. In both cases processing stops. Otherwise the prefix and the trailing : are stripped to get tmSecurityName.

Finally securityParameters is set to a zero-length OCTET STRING (0400), the message parts are combined, and the message and cache reference are returned with success.
sections.eli5: When sending, the checker writes the sticky note: who the message is for and how locked the truck must be. For a reply, it copies the note from the question, so the answer goes back the same safe way.

sections.title: Processing Incoming Messages
sections.content:
For an incoming message TSM sets securityEngineID to the local snmpEngineID. If the tmStateReference does not point to a cache with a transport domain, transport address, tmSecurityName and tmTransportSecurityLevel, it increments snmpTsmInvalidCaches, returns an error and stops. This is what happens if TSM is used with a non-secure Transport Model.

TSM copies tmSecurityName to securityName. If prefixes are enabled, it looks up the prefix for the transport domain (errors increment the unknown or invalid prefix counters) and sets securityName to the prefix, a : and the tmSecurityName.

Next it compares levels. If the requested securityLevel needs privacy but the transport gave none, or needs authentication but the transport gave none, snmpTsmInadequateSecurityLevels is incremented and an unsupportedSecurityLevel error is returned. Otherwise the cache is kept as cachedSecurityData for the response, the scopedPDU is extracted from the message, maxSizeResponseScopedPDU is calculated, and success is returned.
sections.eli5: When a message arrives, the checker reads the name tag, adds the truck-type nickname if the rules say so, and checks the lock is at least as strong as needed. If not, it drops the message and adds a tally mark.

sections.title: The SNMP-TSM-MIB Module
sections.content:
The MIB module is registered at mib-2 190 and is for use only by TSM. It has two subtrees. snmpTsmStats holds four read-only Counter32 error counters: snmpTsmInvalidCaches, snmpTsmInadequateSecurityLevels, snmpTsmUnknownPrefixes and snmpTsmInvalidPrefixes.

snmpTsmConfiguration holds one read-write object, snmpTsmConfigurationUsePrefix. When true, securityNames going to and from the application carry a transport-domain prefix, added for incoming messages and removed for outgoing ones. It defaults to false and SHOULD persist across reboots. The module follows the RFC 3411 habit of self-contained documents, so other documents SHOULD NOT reference these objects.

An entity implementing TSM is assumed to implement the SNMP-FRAMEWORK-MIB, SNMP-TARGET-MIB, SNMP-VIEW-BASED-ACM-MIB and SNMPv2-MIB, though these are not needed to implement the SNMP-TSM-MIB.
sections.eli5: The MIB is a small dashboard. It has one switch for the nickname feature and four tally counters for the kinds of mistakes the checker can spot.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
TSM relies on Transport Models for mutual authentication, binding of keys, confidentiality and integrity. It SHOULD always be used with Transport Models that provide adequate security, but what counts as adequate is a configuration or run-time decision by the operator or management application.

Because Transport Models differ, TSM can be configured to prepend a prefix to the securityName so access decisions can take the authenticating Transport Model into account. For the MIB, the one sensitive object is snmpTsmConfigurationUsePrefix. Changing it could create a denial of service or authorize messages that an access control model such as VACM would not have authorized before. The counters refer to configuration errors and do not expose sensitive information.

The RFC recommends SNMPv3 with cryptographic security and says deploying versions prior to SNMPv3 is NOT RECOMMENDED.
sections.eli5: The checker is only as good as the tunnel it trusts. The nickname switch is sensitive, because flipping it could let in people who were not allowed before.

sections.title: Notification Example and USM Comparison
sections.content:
Appendix A configures a notification originator to send informs to 192.0.2.1:5162 over snmpSSHDomain using the securityName "alice", the Transport Security Model and authPriv. The Transport Security Model finds the Transport Model from snmpTargetAddrTDomain, and that model selects a connection using the tmStateReference built from the address, security name and level.

Appendix B contrasts the order of work. With USM, the Message Processing Model decodes the ASN.1 header first and the Security Model then authenticates, checks integrity and timeliness, and decrypts. With a secure transport, the Transport Model does the authentication, integrity, timeliness and decryption first and translates the identity (for example an SSH user name) into a tmSecurityName, and only then is the ASN.1 header decoded. The Security Model maps that identifier to a securityName.
sections.eli5: With the old way the mail room opens the envelope to see who it is from. With the new way the armored truck checks the sender at the door before the envelope is opened.

viz.caption: WHO DOES WHAT FIRST: USM VERSUS A SECURE TRANSPORT

cells: Authenticate, check integrity and timeliness, decrypt
Security Model, after the header is decoded

items.label: snmpTsmInvalidCaches
items.desc: Incoming messages dropped because tmStateReference referred to an invalid cache.

items.label: snmpTsmInadequateSecurityLevels
items.desc: Incoming messages dropped because the transport's securityLevel was less than requested.

items.label: snmpTsmUnknownPrefixes
items.desc: Messages dropped because prefixes were enabled but none is known for the transport domain.

items.label: snmpTsmInvalidPrefixes
items.desc: Messages dropped because an outgoing securityName lacked a valid prefix.

items.label: snmpTsmConfigurationUsePrefix
items.desc: Read-write switch for transport-domain prefixes; defaults to false.
